title: Using tensorflow to automatically compute gradients w.r.t. spectral decomposition error
description:
Hi,

I'm having issues with evaluating the gradients of eigenvalues/eigenvectors with respect to the underlying matrix. Tensorflow evaluates the gradients, however when compared against analytical derivations and numerical (finite difference approx.) differentiation the gradients are generally inconsistent (I understand numerical can be unstable). I'd like to understand is there's a bug in the gradients or if a different methodology was employed to the one cited below.

We are using tf.self_adjoint_eig to evaluate the spectral decomposition for the tensorflow variable input. The input to this is symmetric so this gives the correct eigenvalues and eigenvectors. 

The analytical gradients of eigenvalues and vectors can be found in the paper "On differentiating Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors" by Magnus, Theorem 1 eqn (6) + (7). For the eigenvalues, the gradients are similar, however the eigenvectors are off by quite a bit outside the diagonal entries. To start, define a matrix A as (excuse the matrix output formatting from R)

        [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]   -3   -2    4
[2,]   -2    1    1
[3,]    4    1    5

we can find the spectral decomposition as 

eigen() decomposition
$values
[1]  6.661666  1.769050 -5.430716

$vectors
          [,1]                    [,2]                 [,3]
[1,] 0.3769768 -0.31452619 -0.8711841
[2,] 0.0303395  0.94426587 -0.3277827
[3,] 0.9257257  0.09713517  0.3655089

We now wish to find the gradients of the third eigenvalue (-5.430716) with respect to A. 

[1] "Analytical gradient:"

           [,1]                   [,2]             [,3]
[1,]  0.7589618  0.2855591 -0.3184255
[2,]  0.2855591  0.1074415 -0.1198075
[3,] -0.3184255 -0.1198075  0.1335967

[1] "Numerical gradient:"

            [,1]                     [,2]                  [,3]
[1,]  0.75896178 -0.29699635 -0.03055155
[2,] -0.29699635  0.10744148  0.09172142
[3,] -0.03055155  0.09172142  0.13359674

[1] "Tensorflow gradient:"
[[1]]
           [,1]                  [,2]             [,3]
[1,]  0.7589618  0.0000000 0.0000000
[2,]  0.5711181  0.1074415 0.0000000
[3,] -0.6368511 -0.2396150 0.1335967

The lower triangle of the analytical gradient is exactly half of the tensorflow evaluated gradient. We have done the same thing with the gradients of the eigenvectors. Suppose we wish to take the gradient of element (2,3) in the eigenvector matrix (-0.3277827). I have taken individual elements since tensorflow aggregates gradients if the output is a vector. Results below:

[1] "Analytical gradient:"

            [,1]                      [,2]                   [,3]
[1,] -0.03511309 -0.013211284  0.014731839
[2,]  0.10795607  0.040618426 -0.045293411
[3,]  0.01312188  0.004937104 -0.005505341

[1] "Numerical gradient:"

             [,1]                       [,2]                 [,3]
[1,]  0.035113085  0.03524435  0.003625532
[2,] -0.004634473 -1.19683265  0.001431265
[3,]  0.007039400 -0.02113358 38.853658605

 "Tensorflow gradient:"

              [,1]                   [,2]                     [,3]
[1,] -0.03511309  0.00000000  0.000000000
[2,]  0.09474478  0.04061843  0.000000000
[3,]  0.02785372 -0.04035631 -0.005505341

Note that the diagonals of the tensorflow and analytical align, however the off diagonals are not quite right. The code below should reproduce the output above. Any insight into this would be appreciated.

### System information
- **Have I written custom code (as opposed to using a stock example script provided in TensorFlow)**: YES
- **OS Platform and Distribution (e.g., Linux Ubuntu 16.04)**: macOS High Sierra 10.13.1
- **TensorFlow installed from (source or binary)**: pip install tensor flow
- **TensorFlow version (use command below)**: v1.2.0-5-g435cdfc 1.2.1
- **Python version**: 3.5.2
- **Bazel version (if compiling from source)**: N/A
- **GCC/Compiler version (if compiling from source)**: N/A
- **CUDA/cuDNN version**: N/A
- **GPU model and memory**: N/A 


`########### Start program ########### 

library(tensorflow)

#create upper triangular matrix
A_vec = c(-3,-2,4,-2,1,1,4,1,5)
A = matrix(A_vec, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
e = eigen(A)
#extract eigenvalues and eigenvectors
e_val = e$values
e_vec = e$vectors

#tensorflow variables
A_tf = tf$Variable(tf$constant(A))
e_tf = tf$self_adjoint_eig(A_tf)
#extract eigenvalues and eigenvectors
e_val_tf = e_tf[[1]]
e_vec_tf = e_tf[[2]]

#initialise variables and run session
sess = tf$Session()
sess$run(tf$global_variables_initializer())

#show eigenvalues for Tensorflow and R
print("Tensorflow eigenvalues:")
sess$run(e_tf[[1]])
print("R eigenvalues:") 
e$values

############# Eigenvector element gradient #############

####from the above, index 3 in R is the same as index 1 in TF. Select this to take gradient w.r.t. A

eval_grad_tf = tf$gradients(e_val_tf[1], A_tf) #Tensorflow gradient

#numerical differentiation
eigenval <- function(X_vec){
  X = matrix(X_vec,c(3,3))
  return(eigen(X)$values[3])
}

eval_grad_num = grad(eigenval, A_vec) #gradient of the 3rd eigenvalue from R output
eval_grad_num = matrix(eval_grad_num,c(3,3))

#analytical gradient 
eigenvec3 = eigen(A)$vectors[,3]

#analytical deriv from analytical gradient of eigenvalue from Magnus (1985), "On differentiating
#Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors", Theorem 1 eqn (6)
eval_grad_analytical = outer(eigenvec3,eigenvec3)

print("Analytical gradient:")
eval_grad_analytical
print("Numerical gradient:")
eval_grad_num
print("Tensorflow gradient:")
sess$run(eval_grad_tf)

############# Eigenvector element gradient #############

#numerical differentiation

###from above, eigenvector 3 in R is the negative of eigenvector 1 in Tensorflow

evec_grad_tf = tf$gradients(e_vec_tf[2,1], A_tf) #Tensorflow gradient

#numerical differentiation
eigenvec <- function(X_vec){
  X = matrix(X_vec,c(3,3))
  return(eigen(X)$vectors[2,3])
}

evec_grad_num = grad(eigenvec, A_vec) #gradient of the 3rd eigenvalue from R output
evec_grad_num = matrix(evec_grad_num,c(3,3))

#analytical gradient 

#analytical deriv from analytical gradient of eigenvalue from Magnus (1985), "On differentiating
#Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors", Theorem 1 eqn (7)
evec_grad_analytical = kronecker(eigenvec3, ginv(e_val[3]*diag(3)-A)) #calculates derivatives for each component of eigenvector 3
evec_grad_analytical3 = matrix(evec_grad_analytical[,2],c(3,3)) #retrieves column 2 which should correspond to the gradient of eigenvector 3 element 2 w.r.t. A

print("Analytical gradient:")
evec_grad_analytical3
print("Numerical gradient:")
evec_grad_num
print("Tensorflow gradient:")
sess$run(evec_grad_tf)
`

title: Consider 1-based indexing for tensor [ operator
description:
I've recently been working on some Keras examples that mix use of R/NumPy arrays and raw TF tensor objects. Within the code the same data is accessed via the `[` operator in both contexts. However, one context is 0-based and the other is 1-based. 

This makes for an incredibly confusing situation, and that's for me the maintainer of all of these packages! I wonder if we should revisit our decision to use 0-based indexing for the  tensor`[` operator. The original motivation was two-fold:

1) The other lower-level `tf$` functions use 0-based indexing; and

2) If you were porting Python code that used 0-based indexing then this would ease the porting.

However, I wonder if the case of mixed R array and TF tensor access will be more common. I think it's a reasonably clean story to say that *as a convenience* we make TF tensors 1-based when using the R `[` operator. This is in fact more semantically consistent with `[`, in which AFAICT 0 is equivalent to dropping a dimension.

If we did this we could detect 0 based indexes and yield an error from them (with a note describing how to put the package in backward compatibility mode via an option). I realize that this would cause some short-term pain, but if 1-based is really the right long term direction it's much better that we do it now.

@goldingn I am particularly interested in your opinion about this.

title: Combining exogenous data
description:
I was looking through the examples on the R-Studio/Keras website, but could not find a clear example of combining exogenous features to a model.

```
library(data.table)

K <- backend()

# prepare Y data

title: Virtualenv installation tries to fetch nonexistent package "pip3" when python version is >=3.0
description:
When python version is >= 3.0 The binary name stored in "pip_version" gets passed as a package name to "pip_install()', resulting in the following error after running `install_tensorflow()`

> Upgrading pip ...
> Collecting pip3
>   Could not find a version that satisfies the requirement pip3 (from versions: )
> No matching distribution found for pip3
> Error: Error 1 occurred installing TensorFlow

The fix appears to be simply to hardcode "pip" as a package name in the `pip_install()` call, as I suggest in pull request #172  .

```
library(tensorflow) # execute this line
tf$con<TAB>
```

You should see completions pop up. Then, try finishing the rest of by typing `rib` (to complete `tf$contrib`). Then, try typing `$<TAB>` to get completions within the `contrib` module.

After doing this, I see a bunch of warnings in the console of the form:

< ... >

```
    # Filter annoying Cython warnings that serve no good purpose.

    warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="numpy.ufunc size changed")
    warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="numpy.ndarray size changed")
```

Indeed, within RStudio, the warning filter list is empty in my case:

```
> warnings <- import("warnings")
> warnings$filters
list()
```

But, within a Python session after loading `numpy`, I see some warning filters:

```
>>> import numpy
>>> warnings.filters
[('ignore', <_sre.SRE_Pattern object at 0x10d501670>, <type 'exceptions.Warning'>, <_sre.SRE_Pattern object at 0x10d5c1db0>, 0), ('ignore', <_sre.SRE_Pattern object at 0x10d758880>, <type 'exceptions.Warning'>, <_sre.SRE_Pattern object at 0x10d5c1db0>, 0), ('ignore', <_sre.SRE_Pattern object at 0x10d758750>, <type 'exceptions.Warning'>, <_sre.SRE_Pattern object at 0x10d5c1db0>, 0), ('ignore', <_sre.SRE_Pattern object at 0x10d56a468>, <type 'exceptions.DeprecationWarning'>, <_sre.SRE_Pattern object at 0x10c9c9d98>, 0), ('always', None, <class 'numpy.lib.polynomial.RankWarning'>, None, 0), ('ignore', None, <type 'exceptions.DeprecationWarning'>, None, 0), ('ignore', None, <type 'exceptions.PendingDeprecationWarning'>, None, 0), ('ignore', None, <type 'exceptions.ImportWarning'>, None, 0), ('ignore', None, <type 'exceptions.BytesWarning'>, None, 0)]

Is it possible that TensorFlow, or reticulate, is accidentally clearing out the filter list when running some Python code?

title: install_tensorflow() documentation and test coverage should be more explicit about Python binary expectations
description:
I recently submitted https://github.com/rstudio/tensorflow/pull/153 when my local install of Python failed the install_tensorflow() assumptions. As this is meant to be a "convenience method", I would recommend that the documentation for using this install method be more explicit about the expectations of where it expects Python to live (ie, it only works with a system python installed in /usr/bin or /usr/local/bin). If someone is a pyenv user, I think we can assume they can follow the alternate instructions, but it needs to be more explicit.

Additionally, it was mentioned in the response that using "which" failed in certain scenarios including MacOS with homebrew. My recommendation would be to add test coverage for this scenario so that someone else coming along and submitting this patch sees very clearly the pitfalls of a similar approach. TravisCI offers the ability to test on different platforms, so if MacOS is the problem child, then you should be able to replicate the failing homebrew scenario.

Installation methods documentation:
https://tensorflow.rstudio.com/installation.html#installation_methods

title: Is there full float16 support?
description:
Hi again,

I set dtype =tf$float16 in the below code:
```
require(tensorflow)
sess = tf$InteractiveSession()

# Settings
nSeq  = 1000
nDat  = 5
train = array(replicate(nDat, rnorm(nSeq)), dim = c(nDat, nSeq, 1))
targ  = as.matrix(rnorm(nDat))

nHidden = 6
nLayers = 2
dtype  = tf$float16

# Set up NN graph
data   = tf$placeholder(dtype, shape(NULL, nSeq, 1))
target = tf$placeholder(dtype, shape(NULL, 1))

cells  = lapply(1:nLayers, function(i){ tf$nn$rnn_cell$LSTMCell(nHidden, state_is_tuple = T) })
m_cell = tf$nn$rnn_cell$MultiRNNCell(cells, state_is_tuple = T)
out    = tf$nn$dynamic_rnn(m_cell, data, dtype = dtype)[[1]]

out  = tf$transpose(out, shape(1, 0, 2))
last = tf$gather(out, as.integer(nSeq - 1))

weights = tf$Variable(tf$truncated_normal(shape(nHidden, 1), dtype = dtype))
bias    = tf$Variable(tf$truncated_normal(shape(1), dtype = dtype))

pred       = tf$matmul(last, weights) + bias
loss       = tf$reduce_mean(tf$square(pred - target))
train_step = tf$train$AdamOptimizer(1e-4)$minimize(loss)

# Run
sess$run(tf$global_variables_initializer())
train_step$run(feed_dict = dict(data = train, target = targ))
sess$run(pred, dict(data = train))
```

This gives me the following error at the final line:
```
Error in py_ref_to_r(x) : 
  Conversion from numpy array type 23 is not supported
```

It seems to work (I don't get the error) if I instead use tf$float32 or tf$float64. Is this a bug, really unsupported, or am I doing something wrong?

title: Input MultiRNNCell to dynamic_rnn

In case the content there changes, the relevant python is:
```
import tensorflow

num_units = 200
num_layers = 3
dropout = tf.placeholder(tf.float32)

cells = []
for _ in range(num_layers):
  cell = tf.contrib.rnn.GRUCell(num_units)  # Or LSTMCell(num_units)
  cell = tf.contrib.rnn.DropoutWrapper(cell, output_keep_prob=1.0 - dropout)

cell = tf.contrib.rnn.MultiRNNCell(cells)

title: unexpected behavior when extracting from tensors with undefined shape
description:
Suppose I have a placeholder like `x` define below and I want to extract the first column:

```
x <- tf$placeholder(tf$int16, shape = list(NULL, 1L))
x[,0L]
```
This returns the following error:

```
Error in pmin(end, x_size) : 
  (list) object cannot be coerced to type 'double'
```

The equivalent python code works fine:

```
x = tf.placeholder(tf.int16, [None, 1])
x[:,0]
<tf.Tensor 'strided_slice:0' shape=(?,) dtype=int16>
```
Also the following works as expected:

```
> x <- tf$placeholder(tf$int16, shape = list(1L, 1L))
> x[,0L]
Tensor("StridedSlice:0", shape=(1,), dtype=int16)
```

title: Calling `sess$run` inside a function when tensorflow graph lives in global workspace returns error
description:
I used this code and it did work recently (with an older version of R and tensorflow - now I have R 3.4 and tensorflow 0.8.7)

```
library(tensorflow)
x = tf$placeholder("float", shape(NULL, 2))
W1 = tf$Variable(tf$random_uniform(shape(2, 1), 0, 0.01))
y = tf$matmul(x, W1)
sess = tf$Session()
sess$run(tf$global_variables_initializer())

predict = function(x_) {
  sess$run(y, feed_dict = dict(x = x_))
}
predict(x_ = matrix(c(1, 2), ncol = 2))
```

Now this fails with Error: 
**TypeError: Cannot interpret feed_dict key as Tensor: The name 'x' looks like an (invalid) Operation name, not a Tensor. Tensor names must be of the form "<op_name>:<output_index>".**

When I put the placeholders x and y into the predict function it does work

```
predict = function(x, y, x_) {
  sess$run(y, feed_dict = dict(x = x_))
}
predict(x, y, x_ = matrix(c(1, 2), ncol = 2))
```

Is this a bug or desired behaviour?

title: Rstudio can't use the GPU version of Tensorflow but R in command line can
description:
Hi,

As the title describes, I successfully installed Tensorflow through the package, upgraded it to the GPU version, runs fine in Python and R called from bash, but doesn't work with Rstudio... Below are the details:

I'm running on Ubuntu 16.04 with CUDA 8.0 and CUdnn 5.1 installed.

I successfully installed the CPU version of Tensorflow through R with the instruction you provided:
```R
library(tensorflow)
install_tensorflow()
```
and it worked. Since R calls Tensorflow through a Python API, I thought I might as well replace it with the GPU version and get much faster compute speed. 

So I did a 
```bash
sudo -H pip install --upgrade  $TF_PYTHON_URL
```
where `$TF_PYTHON_URL` points to the url for the python 3.6 GPU version `.whl` file. The installation went successfully, and I was able to do `python -c 'import tensorflow as tf; sess = tf.InteractiveSession()'` and get the log stating that Tensorflow was successfully initialized with my GPUs.

Then under the `r-tensorflow` Conda environment, I entered `R` through command line, and tried 
```R
library(tensorflow)
sess <- tf$InteractiveSession()
```
and it worked! I saw the exact same message as the python call.

However, when I entered RStudio, the same call would fail as RStudio raises error:
```
Error: Installation of TensorFlow not found.
Python environments searched for 'tensorflow' package:
 /home/user/anaconda3/envs/r-tensorflow/bin/python3.6

...
```

so it did search inside the `r-tensorflow` Conda environment and didn't find Tensorflow.

I did a little more research and saw that the R Tensorflow package calls [`import`](https://github.com/rstudio/tensorflow/blob/c1f2fa1b2266497d9c69b3e1ee7c32181955d548/R/package.R#L33) from the [`Reticulate`](https://github.com/rstudio/reticulate/blob/10b4c15db6b614aaa410fc5a37ede2885bcc7ef9/R/python.R#L31) package. I tried running 
```
import("tensorflow")
```

and it gave me the following error:
```
Error in py_module_import(module, convert = convert) : 
  ImportError: Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/user/anaconda3/envs/r-tensorflow/lib/python3.6/site-packages/tensorflow/python/pywrap_tensorflow.py", line 41, in <module>

title: Re-using variables
description:
Hi,

This is related to issue #98. I could not find a way of satisfactory addressing this problem, and would highly appreciate any feedback. I have changed things a bit to illustrate the problem as concisely as possible. If I should be posting this somewhere else as this is not at all related to an actual issue of the tensorflow R package, please let me know. 

Here’s the problem: As illustrated in the code below, I’m calling the `inference` function twice, first on pre-processed images and second on non-pre-processed images. The problem is that by doing so, I’m creating a new set of parameters. I’d like to avoid this behaviour, by sharing the same parameters. That is, I need re-use the parameters obtained from training to make inference on test data.

```r
### Generate random image data
set.seed(1)
N_IMAGES = 100
images <- array(runif(32*32*3 * N_IMAGES) * 250, dim = c(N_IMAGES, 32, 32, 3))
images.lab <- sample(1L:10L, N_IMAGES, replace = TRUE)
labels <- matrix(0L, nrow = N_IMAGES, ncol = 10)
for (i in 1:N_IMAGES) {
  labels[i, ][images.lab[[i]]] <- 1
}
rm(images.lab)

### Create artificial train/test (same in this case as it's just for illustration)
images_train <- images
labels_train <- labels
images_test <- images
labels_test <- labels

### Initialize session
library(tensorflow)
sess <- tf$InteractiveSession()

### Image pre-processing (different for train/test)
pre_process_image <- function(image, train_bool = TRUE) {
  
  if (train_bool) {
    distorted_image <- tf$map_fn(tf$image$per_image_standardization, image)
  } else {
    distorted_image <- image
  }
  distorted_image
}

### Inference op.
inference <- function(image) {
  
  W_conv1 <- tf$Variable(tf$truncated_normal(shape = shape(5L, 5L, 3L, 64L), stddev=5e-2))
  b_conv1 <- tf$Variable(tf$constant(0.1, shape = shape(64L)))
  h_conv1 <- tf$nn$relu(tf$nn$conv2d(image, W_conv1, strides = c(1L, 1L, 1L, 1L), padding = 'SAME') + b_conv1)

  h_pool1 <- tf$nn$max_pool(h_conv1, ksize = c(1L, 3L, 3L, 1L), strides = c(1L, 2L, 2L, 1L), padding = 'SAME')

  W_fc1 <- tf$Variable(tf$truncated_normal(shape = shape(16L * 16L * 64L, 10L), stddev=5e-2))
  b_fc1 <- tf$Variable(tf$constant(0.1, shape = shape(10L)))
  h_pool2_flat <- tf$reshape(h_pool1, shape(-1L, 16L * 16L * 64L))
  y_conv <- tf$matmul(h_pool2_flat, W_fc1) + b_fc1
  y_conv
}

### Model evaluation
evaluation <- function(logits, labels) {
  correct_prediction <- tf$equal(tf$argmax(logits, 1L), tf$argmax(labels, 1L))
  accuracy <- tf$reduce_mean(tf$cast(correct_prediction, tf$float32))
  accuracy
}

### Placeholders
x <- tf$placeholder(tf$float32, shape(NULL, 32L, 32L, 3L))
y_true <- tf$placeholder(tf$float32, shape(NULL, 10L))
x_image <- tf$reshape(x, shape(-1L, 32L, 32L, 3L))

### Set-up training op. on pre-processed images
x_image_pp <- pre_process_image(x_image, train_bool = TRUE)
y_conv <- inference(x_image_pp)
cross_entropy <- tf$nn$softmax_cross_entropy_with_logits(labels = y_true, logits = y_conv) 
optimizer <- tf$train$AdamOptimizer(learning_rate = 0.0001)
global_step <- tf$Variable(0L, name = 'global_step', trainable = FALSE)
train_step <- optimizer$minimize(cross_entropy, global_step = global_step)

### Evaluation on non-pre-processed images 
x_image_pp_te <- pre_process_image(x_image, train_bool = FALSE)
y_conv_te <- inference(x_image_pp_te) ### Here's the issue...NOT re-using the already trained model
accuracy <- evaluation(y_conv_te, y_true)

### Training parameters
batch_size = 20L
max_steps = 10

sess$run(tf$global_variables_initializer())

for (i in 1:max_steps) {
  
  ind <- sample(1:100, batch_size, replace = FALSE)
  x_batch = images_train[ind,,,]
  y_batch = labels_train[ind, ]
  sess$run(train_step, feed_dict = dict(x = x_batch, y_true = y_batch))
  if (i %% 1 == 0) {
    acc_test <- sess$run(accuracy, feed_dict = dict(
      x = images_test, y_true = labels_test))
    cat(sprintf("Test Accuracy at step %s: %s \n", i, acc_test))
    
  }
}
``` 

Thanks,
Lars.

title: Should 'parse_flags()' return a dictionary / list of flags?
description:
E.g. the example I'm porting looks like this:

```python
< ... >
args = parser.parse_args()
arguments = args.__dict__
learn_runner.run(generate_experiment_fn(**arguments), job_dir)
```

We could mimic this with R code like:

```R
< ... >
parse_flags()
arguments = tf$flags$FLAGS$`__dict__`$`__flags`
experiment_fn <- do.call(generate_experiment_fn, arguments)
learn_runner$run(experiment_fn, job_dir)
```

But unpacking the flags in that way is pretty ugly. I would propose that our `parse_flags()` function return the dictionary / list of arguments directly, e.g.

```R
arguments <- parse_flags()
experiment_fn <- do.call(generate_experiment_fn, arguments)
learn_runner$run(experiment_fn, job_dir)
```

title: Inconsistency between tf.matmul in Python and tf$matmul in R
description:
Attached is a simple example of an issue in using matmul to multiply an array of matrices in R.  I think the issue is a discrepancy in the way that the shape argument works in the R and python version.  

I am trying to use the tf$matmul function to multiply an array of matrices by an array of vectors.  As an example, I am trying to multiply [1, 2; 3, 4] * [1; 2] and [5,6; 7,8] * [3; 4].  The example works as expected in Python, but in the TensorFlow API for R, a dimension error is generated.  

In Python, the code for the example is:
############# Beginning of Python code
import tensorflow as tf
a = tf.constant(np.arange(1, 9, dtype=np.int32),shape=[2, 2, 2])  #create array of 2 matrices each 2x2: (1,2; 3,4) and (5,6; 7,8)
b = tf.constant(np.arange(1, 5, dtype=np.int32),shape=[2, 2, 1]) #multuply each of the matrices by a 2x1 vector (1,2)' and (3,4)' 
sess = tf.Session()
sess.run(a)
c = tf.matmul(a, b)
sess.run(a)
sess.run(b)
sess.run(c)  #the answer is the correct set of 2x1 vectors (5,11)' and (39,53)'
############# End of Python Code

When I try to implement this same example in R, an error is produced due to a difference in the way the dimensions of the arrays are indexed in the shape argument.  

##################### Begin R Code
rm(list = ls())
devtools::install_github("rstudio/tensorflow")
library(tensorflow)

#Create an array of 3 matrices
A = list(matrix(1:4, nrow=2, byrow=T), matrix(5:8, nrow=2, byrow=T))
A = array(unlist(A), dim=c(2,2,2) )  #2 matrices of dimension 2x2
B = array(1:4, dim = c(2,1,2) )  #2 vectors of 2x1
A_tf = tf$constant(A, dtype="float64", shape=c(2,2,2))  
B_tf = tf$constant(B, dtype="float64", shape=c(2,1,2))
sess = tf$Session()
sess$run(A_tf)
sess$run(B_tf)
sess$run(tf$matmul(A_tf,B_tf))

################## End R code

I believe the error is because of a discrepancy in the way that the shape argument works in tf$constant (R) and the way the shape argument works in tf.constant (R).  In R, the number of elements in the array is the last argument in shape so that  shape = c(2,1,3) means an array with 3 2x1 vectors.  In the python implementation, the number of array elements is the first argument so that shape=[3, 2, 1]  means 3 vectors of 2x1.  

When the function tf$matmul(A_tf,B_tf) is called, I think the difference in indexing the shapes of the array is causing an error. 

Thanks for your attention.

train_accuracy <- accuracy$eval(feed_dict = dict(
  x = batch[[1]], y_ = batch[[2]], keep_prob = 1.0))

  x = batch[[1]], y_ = batch[[2]], keep_prob = 0.5))
train_accuracy <- accuracy$eval(feed_dict = dict(

for these ones:

train_accuracy <- accuracy$eval(session=sess, feed_dict = dict(

train_step$run(session=sess, feed_dict = dict(

train_accuracy <- accuracy$eval(session=sess, feed_dict = dict(

description:

I have a model
```
# Parameters
...

# Model
layer1 = tf$add(tf$matmul(x, weight_variable(shape(n_input, n_hidden_1))),
                bias_variable(shape(n_hidden_1)))
layer1 = tf$nn$relu(layer1)

layer2 = tf$add(tf$matmul(layer1, weight_variable(shape(n_hidden_1, n_hidden_2))),
                bias_variable(shape(n_hidden_2)))
layer2 = tf$nn$relu(layer2)

out_layer = tf$matmul(layer2, weight_variable(shape(n_hidden_2, n_classes))) +
            bias_variable(shape(n_classes))

# Initialize graph
sess <- tf$Session()
sess$run(tf$initialize_all_variables())

# Train
...
```

I use `out_layer` to make a prediction like this:
```
pred = sess$run(out_layer, feed_dict = dict(x = test.x))
```

later I save the model like this:

```
saver <- tf$train$Saver()
data_file <- saver$save(sess, paste0(data.dir, "my_model.ckpt"))
```

Then I restart R (to test if restoring works). This leads to the situation that now all tensorflow objects are \<Object with null pointer>.
Now I **try** to restore the model like this:

```
sess = tf$Session()
restorer = tf$train$import_meta_graph(paste0(data.dir, "my_model.ckpt.meta"))
restorer$restore(sess, tf$train$latest_checkpoint(data.dir))
```
...this gives me no errors.
However, `out_layer` (and the other tensorflow-objects) is still an \<Object with null pointer>! Does this mean, restoring the model has not really worked, or do I just have to make an effort to assign `out_layer` the correct pointer again?

title: Passing lists of tensors as arguments
description:
Hi all

Some tf functions expect a Python list of Tensors as an argument, e.g. tf.concat() and tf.pack(). Is there any elegant way to pass an R list of tensors to these functions? Simply using `tf$concat(concat_dim = 1, values = list(t1, t2), name = "concat1")` throws an error - I believe because the Tensors are passed as a tuple instead of a list.

I'm currently using the following (admittedly ugly) workaround:
```R
tf_concatenate <- function(tf, concat_dim, t1, t2, name) {
  tensorflow:::py_run_string("def tfcc(tf, concat_dim, t1, t2, name):
    return tf.concat(concat_dim, [t1, t2], name)")
  mn <- tensorflow::import("__main__")
  mn$tfcc(tf, as.integer(concat_dim), t1, t2, name)
}
```

title: Memory issue?
description:
I see excessive memory use transferring numeric objects between R and Python. I'm trying to track this down in the source now.

```{r}
packageDescription("tensorflow")
# Version: 0.3.0
# Date: 2016-10-11
# Built: R 3.3.1; x86_64-pc-linux-gnu; 2016-11-03 18:41:44 UTC; unix
# RemoteRepo: tensorflow
# RemoteRef: master
# RemoteSha: f85748ec526c4ff4d6e400ef8a8c92abea6d27c8
```

Tiny example:
```{r}
library(tensorflow)
np <- import("numpy")
x <- runif(2e8)
object.size(x)
# 1600000200 bytes

x <- np$array(x)
rm(x)
gc()
```
Ideally this would use maybe 3.2GB RAM, or at worst I expect something like 4.8GB. But on my system this takes over 10 GB resident RAM, and consumes 4.6 GB resident RAM even after the gc() after deleting the data. The good news is that the residual RAM use does not seem to be a leak, it's maybe just a hidden cache somewhere. Still, a >2x worst-case memory overhead is a bit excessive, right? That kind of rules out sharing anything but relatively small objects.

title: installation issue with Anaconda on Mac
description:
I'm so excited to have an R interface. Thanks so much for building this.

Unfortunately, it doesn't seem to work on my machine yet.  After what seems like a successful install (see installation messages at the bottom of this post), I get the following message when I try to load it in RStudio:

```
>library(tensorflow)
TensorFlow not currently installed, please see https://www.tensorflow.org/get_started/
```

My best guess is that it's an Anaconda issue?  Here's what I get when I type `python` at the bash prompt:

```
Python 2.7.11 |Anaconda 2.4.0 (x86_64)| (default, Dec  6 2015, 18:57:58) 
[GCC 4.2.1 (Apple Inc. build 5577)] on darwin
```

Tensorflow works from Python (I've used it via the `keras` package). I've copied its location in my file directory below:

```
>>> import tensorflow as tf
>>> tf
<module 'tensorflow' from '/Users/davidharris/anaconda/lib/python2.7/site-packages/tensorflow/__init__.pyc'>
```

Let me know if I can provide any additional information that would help debug this.  Thanks again!

title: installation failure on OS X with homebrew python
description:
(Sorry if I'm reporting this prematurely / this isn't expected to work yet!)

When attempting to build on OS X, I see a build during execution of `.onLoad()`, etc.

```
